work.title: Workvivo HQ
work.summary: Repositioning employee experience for the AI era—without losing the adoption, trust, and culture that made the platform distinctive.
work.demonstrates: Platform repositioning, category evolution, executive narrative, launch strategy, and buyer storytelling across IT, HR, and Comms.
work.proof: Public launch page, 60-slide pitch deck, campaign system, Shauna launch post, and public peer testimonial.

caseStudy.eyebrow: Repositioning a category for the AI era
caseStudy.context: Workvivo had established itself as an Employee Experience Platform. As enterprise software moved into an AI-native era, the challenge was bigger than adding AI features to the existing story: the company needed a credible new ambition without abandoning the employee-experience equity that made it distinctive.
caseStudy.challenge: What should Workvivo become when AI changes how employees interact with information, systems, and work? A generic ‘we’re now an AI company’ claim would have discarded the adoption, culture, frontline reach, and trust the platform had already earned.
caseStudy.insight: AI becomes more valuable when it lives inside an employee experience people already use. The platform story shifted toward an AI-native headquarters for every employee, captured in the central idea: Give work a home.
contribution: Strategic positioning and category narrative
Messaging architecture across IT, HR, and Comms buyers
Launch strategy, seller narrative, and website story
Analyst story and competitive framing
Portfolio narrative connecting Workvivo HQ to the broader AI strategy
decisions: Position AI as embedded in the employee experience—not bolted on
Make adoption part of the AI ROI story
Frame one destination where employees can understand, find, and increasingly act
Keep frontline employees inside the enterprise AI narrative
caseStudy.outcome: Workvivo publicly launched HQ while serving 9 million users and after surpassing $100M ARR. Those are company proof points during Shauna’s tenure, not outcomes attributed to her alone.
caseStudy.learning: Repositioning works when it expands what a brand can mean without erasing the reason customers trusted it in the first place.

work.title: AI Product Strategy
work.summary: Learning by building: product strategy, AI pricing, portfolio agents, and hands-on experimentation with the tools reshaping modern GTM.
work.demonstrates: AI product judgment, pricing strategy, agent prototyping, workflow design, technical curiosity, and applied PMM experimentation.
work.proof: Product School coursework, AI pricing study, this portfolio agent, and builds using Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Replit, Lovable, ElevenLabs, and ZoomMate.

caseStudy.eyebrow: Building an AI-enabled PMM operating model
caseStudy.context: AI-first Product Marketing is not simply a team using ChatGPT. Shauna has been exploring how AI can change the operating model of PMM itself—and where human judgment must remain accountable.
caseStudy.challenge: High-value PMM time disappears into retrieval, repeated seller questions, monitoring, synthesis, recurring research, and first-pass analysis. The strategic question is which work requires human judgment and which work can be processed or automated.
caseStudy.insight: AI does more of the processing. PMM remains accountable for the thinking. Retrieval, extraction, monitoring, classification, and repeatable analysis can accelerate; positioning, pricing, claims, category strategy, and executive recommendations still need accountable judgment.
contribution: Seller-facing competitive intelligence and automated monitoring
AI-assisted win/loss analysis and lightweight decision tools
AI Positioning QA
This portfolio and its grounded agent experience
Reusable research, synthesis, and PMM workflows
Continued product and AI-pricing study
decisions: Design around workflows rather than collecting tools
Keep a human in the loop for consequential claims and decisions
Encode PMM expertise into evaluation criteria
Use prototypes to learn before deciding whether to build, buy, or stop
caseStudy.outcome: The result is a growing set of practical systems that increase PMM leverage while keeping strategic accountability human. The tools are not the proof; the workflow design and operating choices are.
caseStudy.learning: Technical expertise for a PMM is the ability to understand enough of the system to make better product, pricing, trust, and go-to-market decisions.

work.title: Shauna, Decoded
work.summary: Designing a live voice and text portfolio agent that can route intent, retrieve focused evidence, preserve claim boundaries, and explain the work behind the résumé.
work.demonstrates: Conversational AI, agent workflow design, modular RAG, knowledge architecture, evaluation, claim governance, voice UX, and web integration.
work.proof: Live ElevenLabs agent embedded in this portfolio, versioned knowledge sources and routing rules, a repeatable source-build process, and a documented 13-question evaluation framework.

caseStudy.eyebrow: Turning a résumé into an evidence-grounded conversation
caseStudy.context: A static portfolio can show the work, but it cannot adapt to the question a recruiter, hiring manager, or technical stakeholder actually wants answered. Shauna designed a live ElevenLabs experience that lets visitors explore her career, case studies, technical builds, and working principles through voice or text.
caseStudy.challenge: The agent needed to be persuasive without becoming a hype machine. It had to answer broad career questions quickly, go deep on named projects, distinguish work Shauna built from products she marketed, link back to public evidence, and avoid turning company outcomes or technical fluency into unsupported personal claims.
caseStudy.insight: A credible portfolio agent is primarily a context-and-evaluation problem. Better answers came from separating durable rules from retrievable evidence, routing different intents to specialist answer modes, and testing the hard questions where attribution, role fit, or technical ownership could easily drift.
contribution: Defined the agent's purpose, answer contract, voice, and evidence standard
Designed a modular knowledge base around career, technical builds, case studies, learning, recognition, and a canonical claim ledger
Wrote intent-routing conditions for technical questions, case-study deep dives, career history, working style, and role-fit pressure tests
Created acceptance questions and an adversarial evaluation set covering attribution, unsupported claims, conflicting evidence, and technical boundaries
Integrated the ElevenLabs conversational widget into a responsive GitHub Pages portfolio
Built a Node-based source pipeline that converts maintained Markdown into upload-ready HTML knowledge documents
decisions: Use voice and text as the interface, while keeping public case-study links as the evidence layer
Keep compact identity and claim rules in always-on prompt context; retrieve longer case-study material only when relevant
Route by visitor intent rather than forcing one general prompt to handle every conversation style
Answer technical questions decisively with concrete build evidence, then add ownership boundaries only where they prevent a false inference
Keep knowledge sources versioned in Git so updates are inspectable and repeatable
Treat live platform configuration and repository evidence as separate states; published files document the design but do not prove every console setting is active
architecture: ElevenLabs Conversational AI provides the live voice and text runtime embedded through its web component
A main agent coordinates specialist workflow routes for career, technical evidence, case-study depth, working style, and fit assessment
Two compact prompt documents hold identity, answer policy, and claim controls in persistent context
Nine focused knowledge documents are configured for RAG so the agent retrieves only the evidence relevant to the question
A canonical claim ledger separates externally verified facts, public artifacts, self-reported experience, company context, and work still in progress
Absolute portfolio and repository links let answers point visitors back to inspectable evidence
tooling: ElevenLabs Conversational AI for the agent runtime, speech interface, workflow, and knowledge retrieval
HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript for the portfolio and widget integration
Markdown and structured front matter as the editable knowledge source
Node.js for deterministic Markdown-to-HTML knowledge builds
Git and GitHub for versioning, public evidence, and GitHub Pages deployment
Codex and other AI development tools for implementation support, with Shauna retaining the product, content, and claim decisions
safeguards: Third-person identity prevents the agent from impersonating Shauna
Attribution rules distinguish products marketed, systems built, tools used, and concepts studied
Hard claim rules block invented metrics, sole credit for company outcomes, and unsupported production-engineering claims
Specialist routing reduces context collisions between technical proof, career history, project narratives, and role-fit assessment
Public links and evidence labels make provenance visible instead of asking visitors to trust generated prose
A bounded answer pattern keeps voice responses concise and avoids turning narrow questions into résumé recitations
validation: Fifteen acceptance questions cover the most common recruiter and technical-review journeys
A 13-question evaluation set tests positioning, technical evidence, ownership boundaries, unsupported claims, role-fit nuance, leadership, and concise voice responses
Explicit pass criteria make review repeatable rather than purely subjective
Knowledge documents carry version and review dates so content drift can be traced
Repository checks can validate source completeness and regenerated HTML before the knowledge pack is uploaded
Live conversational quality still requires manual testing in ElevenLabs after knowledge or workflow configuration changes
caseStudy.outcome: The result is a live, inspectable portfolio interface that demonstrates more than familiarity with AI tools. It shows Shauna's ability to design an agent around context, retrieval, routing, evaluation, trust, and user experience—and to translate those technical choices into a clear professional story. The agent runs on ElevenLabs; Shauna configured and integrated the experience rather than engineering the underlying voice models or platform runtime.
caseStudy.learning: The quality of an agent is shaped less by the cleverness of one prompt than by the discipline of its context, routing, evidence, evaluation, and boundaries.

work.title: HQ Agent
work.summary: Turning enterprise search, trusted answers, self-service, and agentic action into one credible product story—and a launch buyers could navigate.
work.demonstrates: Agentic AI positioning, portfolio architecture, trust messaging, packaging, launch orchestration, and enterprise sales enablement.
work.proof: HQ product experience, launch narrative, seller materials, and portfolio positioning connecting Workvivo and Zoom AI.

caseStudy.context: HQ Agent extended Workvivo beyond communications and employee experience into trusted enterprise answers, search, self-service, and agentic task execution. It sat at the intersection of enterprise knowledge, RAG, permissions, employee experience, and Zoom’s broader AI technology.
caseStudy.challenge: The launch could not be reduced to ‘better enterprise search.’ It needed a clear category, a credible trust story, an understandable relationship with Workvivo HQ and ZoomMate, and sustainable packaging for different levels of AI value.
caseStudy.insight: The most useful commercial progression was SEARCH → ANSWER → ACTION: from finding information, to receiving a grounded answer, to increasingly completing the task. The launch idea became: From search, to answer, to job done.
contribution: Product and portfolio positioning
AI maturity story and competitive framing
Pricing and packaging co-developed with the Revenue leader
Seller narrative and enablement
Translation of trust, permissions, citations, and grounding into buyer value
GTM execution across Product, Revenue, and the market
decisions: Market the buyer value of RAG—not the acronym
Use ‘grounded, cited, and permission-aware’ instead of unsafe absolute claims
Differentiate HQ Agent’s employee support from ZoomMate’s deeper productivity use cases
Price levels of AI value rather than charging for novelty
caseStudy.outcome: The result was a portfolio and launch narrative designed to make a technically complex enterprise AI product easier to understand, sell, and evaluate. Shauna shaped the commercial story; she did not engineer the underlying AI system.
caseStudy.learning: Technical depth matters in Product Marketing when it changes the claim, the value, the packaging, or the buyer’s trust.

work.title: Market leadership
work.summary: Creating one connected market-leadership motion across Gartner, Forrester, G2, ClearBox, Gartner Peer Insights, and SoftwareReviews.
work.demonstrates: Analyst relations, competitive intelligence, category design, campaign strategy, and turning external validation into commercial leverage.
work.proof: Gartner and Forrester leadership campaign artifacts, supported by recognition across major analyst and review platforms.

caseStudy.context: Workvivo evolved from an underdog employee app into a recognised Employee Experience Platform and later a broader AI-native employee-experience story. Analyst understanding had to evolve with the product and company narrative.
caseStudy.challenge: Market leadership is not created by a single briefing. It requires a consistent point of view, credible evidence, strong customer proof, disciplined claims, and alignment across products that are evolving at different speeds.
caseStudy.insight: Analyst relations works best as a connected category system—not a calendar of submissions. The analyst narrative, evidence base, competitive position, customer proof, and GTM story need to reinforce one another.
contribution: Analyst narrative and executive storytelling
Briefings and RFI development
Evidence and customer-proof development
Competitive positioning and claims governance
Alignment across Workvivo HQ, HQ Agent, and Seer
Campaign strategy that translated recognition into market-facing proof
decisions: Build a durable category story rather than chase individual rankings
Keep external claims grounded in verifiable evidence
Connect analyst recognition to seller and buyer narratives
Maintain one coherent portfolio story across multiple evaluation contexts
caseStudy.outcome: Workvivo received recognition across Gartner, Forrester, G2, ClearBox, Gartner Peer Insights, and SoftwareReviews. Shauna played a substantial role in the program; independent analysts and reviewers controlled their own outcomes.
caseStudy.learning: Influence without control demands evidence, consistency, and patience. Strong analyst relations makes the company easier to understand before it tries to make it look impressive.

work.title: The Meta Migration
work.summary: Turning a time-bound market disruption into an award-winning commercial motion—while making migration feel credible, differentiated, and low-risk.
work.demonstrates: Migration positioning, competitive differentiation, market messaging, seller strategy, enablement, and fast cross-functional GTM execution.
work.proof: Forrester named Workvivo its 2026 B2B Return on Integration Honors winner for a cross-functional response to a major market disruption. Shauna’s portfolio identifies the recognised programme as the Meta migration and records her significant GTM role; the award is a company outcome.

caseStudy.context: Meta announced the closure of Workplace. Workvivo was named Meta’s only preferred migration partner, creating a major, time-bound market opportunity and a highly visible competitive GTM motion.
caseStudy.challenge: Workvivo had to move quickly while differentiating against competitors, reducing migration risk, addressing customer uncertainty, enabling sellers, and converting a temporary market event into durable commercial opportunity.
caseStudy.insight: The winning story needed to combine urgency with reassurance. Migration could not feel like a technical transfer alone; it needed to feel like a credible path from a closing platform to a stronger long-term employee experience.
contribution: Migration positioning and narrative
Competitive differentiation
Seller strategy and enablement
Market messaging
Cross-functional coordination of the commercial motion
Helping translate the market event into a repeatable customer story
decisions: Lead with a proven, low-risk migration path
Differentiate the destination—not only the transfer process
Equip sellers for a compressed, competitive decision cycle
Balance market urgency with customer confidence
caseStudy.outcome: Forrester named Workvivo its 2026 B2B Return on Integration Honors winner for a companywide response to a major market disruption. Shauna’s portfolio identifies the recognised programme as the Meta migration and records her as a significant GTM contributor. The award is a company outcome; no migration-share or ARR result is attributed to Shauna.

award.title: 2026 B2B Return on Integration Honors
award.description: Forrester recognised Workvivo for creating exceptional business value by aligning product, engineering, sales, marketing, customer success, and partnerships around a major market disruption. Shauna’s portfolio identifies that company programme as the Meta migration.

caseStudy.learning: When a market window is short, clarity and coordination become competitive advantages. The best displacement story makes both the move and the destination feel compelling.

work.title: Seer
work.summary: Building a people-intelligence story around the Listening Gap: the distance between what employees say and what organisations act on.
work.demonstrates: Research synthesis, category narrative, thought leadership, product positioning, and a practical GTM frame for employee intelligence.
work.proof: Seer product materials and the supplied 18-page Listening Gap research report.

caseStudy.context: Workvivo expanded into People Intelligence with Seer, moving into a buyer and category conversation adjacent to its employee-experience strengths.
caseStudy.challenge: Seer could not sound like another survey platform. The story needed to explain how employee feedback moves beyond collection—turning large volumes of qualitative signal into insight that leaders and managers can act on.
caseStudy.insight: The narrative became LISTEN → UNDERSTAND → ACT. The Listening Gap gave the strategy a memorable tension: organisations often collect employee feedback, but struggle to convert what they hear into meaningful action.
contribution: Positioning and GTM strategy
Launch strategy
Pricing and packaging
Competitive strategy
Seller narrative and enablement
Hiring a dedicated PMM to scale execution while retaining senior strategy ownership
decisions: Anchor the story in action—not survey collection
Use AI topic grouping, comment analysis, and sentiment as means to insight
Connect executive reporting with practical manager action
Position against established engagement and listening alternatives
caseStudy.outcome: Seer established a people-intelligence expansion story spanning employee listening, AI-assisted insight, manager intelligence, and action. No unverified Seer revenue or adoption metrics are claimed.
caseStudy.learning: Adjacent-market entry becomes credible when the narrative explains both the new capability and why the existing brand has earned the right to compete.
